essays.title: The Value of Reading
essays.text: Reading is a habit that rewards those who keep it. Every evening I spend half an hour with a book, and the quiet moment helps me escape the noise of daily life. Books open a window to different cultures and offer me a chance to think independently. When I meet a difficult passage, I slow down and take notes, which improves my understanding. Over the years, reading has broadened my horizons and enriched my vocabulary. It also teaches me patience, because a good book cannot be finished in a hurry. I would encourage everyone to develop this habit, since the benefits are far greater than the time it costs.

essays.title: Learning to Manage Time
essays.text: Many students complain that they never have enough time. In my opinion, the problem is not the amount of time but the way we use it. Last term I made a simple plan: I listed every task, decided which one mattered most, and finished it before checking my phone. The result surprised me. I completed my homework earlier and still had energy for basketball. Managing time well does not mean working all day. It means choosing the most important thing and refusing to be disturbed. Once you form this habit, you will feel calmer and more confident, and your grades will improve naturally.

essays.title: What Makes a Good Friend
essays.text: A good friend is not the one who agrees with you all the time. In fact, a true friend dares to point out your mistakes, even though it may cause an awkward moment. I still remember the day my classmate told me that my attitude towards others was rude. I was angry at first, but later I realized she was right. Since then I have learned to listen and to apologize when necessary. Friendship also requires trust and patience. We cannot expect a friend to be perfect, because nobody is. What matters is that you are willing to support each other, especially when one of you is going through a difficult period.

essays.title: A Dinner with My Family
essays.text: In my family, dinner is never just about food. It is the only time when all of us sit down together and share what has happened during the day. My father usually talks about his work, my mother describes the interesting things she has noticed, and I report the progress I have made at school. Sometimes we argue about small matters, but the atmosphere remains warm. I have gradually understood that these ordinary evenings are precious. They remind me that I am loved and supported, no matter how difficult my studies become. When I leave home for university, I will certainly miss this routine.

essays.title: Exercise Changes More Than Your Body
essays.text: Some of my classmates think exercise is a waste of time because it takes them away from their books. I disagree completely. Two years ago I was weak and often caught colds. Then I began to run for twenty minutes every morning. At the beginning it was painful, and I wanted to give up. But after a month I noticed that I could concentrate better in class and that I was no longer tired in the afternoon. Exercise does not only strengthen the body; it also reduces stress and improves mood. For students who sit for long hours, regular activity is necessary rather than optional.

essays.title: Small Actions, Big Difference
essays.text: Protecting the environment sounds like a huge task that only governments can handle. However, ordinary people can make a real difference. I always carry a bottle instead of buying bottled water, and I refuse plastic bags when shopping. My family separates rubbish and recycles paper and glass. These actions seem tiny, but if millions of people follow them, the effect will be enormous. Besides, saving energy is a matter of attitude. Turning off the light when you leave a room costs nothing, yet it reduces waste. The earth does not need a few perfect heroes; it needs millions of responsible citizens.

essays.title: Living with Smartphones
essays.text: Smartphones have changed our lives in ways we could hardly imagine twenty years ago. They allow us to contact friends instantly, pay for goods, and find information within seconds. However, every advantage comes with a price. Many students cannot concentrate because they check their screens every few minutes, and some even feel anxious when the battery is low. In my view, the problem lies not in the device but in our habits. We should set clear limits, for example by keeping the phone away while doing homework. Used wisely, a smartphone is a useful tool; used carelessly, it becomes a master that controls us.

essays.title: Will Artificial Intelligence Replace Us?
essays.text: Artificial intelligence is developing faster than most people expected. It can translate languages, write reports and even compose music. Some worry that machines will replace human workers and that many people will lose their jobs. I think this fear is partly reasonable, but it is also exaggerated. Machines are good at dealing with data and repeating tasks, yet they lack imagination and genuine emotion. A teacher, for instance, does more than pass on knowledge; he or she encourages and comforts students. The wise attitude is to accept the change, learn new skills, and cooperate with technology instead of fighting against it.

essays.title: Why Traditional Culture Matters
essays.text: In recent years, more young people have become interested in traditional culture. They wear traditional clothes, learn classical instruments and visit museums during holidays. I believe this trend is valuable. Traditions remind us who we are and where we come from. Without them, a society may become rich in material terms but poor in spirit. Of course, we should not simply copy the past. Instead, we ought to understand the meaning behind the customs and combine it with modern life. When a young designer uses traditional patterns in her work, she is not repeating history; she is giving it a new life.

essays.title: A Book That Changed My Mind
essays.text: Last year I read a book about a doctor who worked in a remote village. He had few tools and little money, but he never gave up on his patients. The story impressed me deeply. Before reading it, I had always measured success by salary and reputation. Now I understand that contribution matters more than position. The doctor did not become famous, yet he earned the respect of everyone around him. The book did not offer any easy answers, but it raised questions I had never asked myself. Sometimes a single book is enough to change the direction of a person's thinking.

essays.title: A Meaningful Summer
essays.text: Last summer I joined a volunteer programme and taught children in a mountain village. The conditions were far from comfortable: no air conditioning, limited water, and a long walk to the school. On the first day I was nervous, because I had never stood in front of a class. Gradually I learned to explain things clearly and to encourage shy students. What impressed me most was their curiosity. They asked questions that I could not always answer, which pushed me to prepare more carefully. The experience taught me responsibility and gave me confidence. I returned home tired but grateful.

essays.title: Travel Teaches Tolerance
essays.text: Travel is often described as a way to relax, but I think its greatest value is education. When you visit a strange city, you must deal with unfamiliar food, different customs and unexpected problems. You may get lost, miss a train or misunderstand a local expression. These difficulties force you to become flexible. I once spent a week in a small town where almost nobody spoke English. By the end of the trip I had learned to communicate with gestures and simple words, and I had made several friends. Travel reminds us that our own way of living is not the only reasonable one.

essays.title: Dealing with Failure
essays.text: Nobody enjoys failure, but everybody experiences it. When I failed an important examination last year, I felt ashamed and refused to talk about it. For several days I could not concentrate on anything. Later my teacher asked me a simple question: what have you learned from it? That question changed my attitude. I analyzed my weak points, made a new plan and asked classmates for help. This time I did much better. Failure is painful, but it is also honest; it shows exactly where we need to improve. Those who avoid failure usually avoid growth as well.

essays.title: Setting a Goal
essays.text: Many students say they want to succeed, but few of them can describe what success means to them. A vague dream cannot guide daily decisions. Two years ago I decided that I wanted to study medicine, and suddenly my priorities became clear. I paid more attention to biology, read articles about health, and even volunteered in a hospital. The goal did not make my life easier, but it made it meaningful. Of course, plans may change. However, having a direction is better than wandering aimlessly. A clear goal turns ordinary effort into progress.

essays.title: The Power of Teamwork
essays.text: Last term our class organized a charity sale. At first everyone had different ideas and the discussion turned into an argument. Then our teacher suggested that we divide the work according to our strengths. Those who were good at drawing designed the posters, careful students managed the money, and outgoing students talked to customers. The event was a great success. I learned that teamwork does not mean that everyone does the same thing. It means that each member contributes what he or she does best, and that differences are treated as resources rather than obstacles.

essays.title: Shopping Online: Convenience and Caution
essays.text: Online shopping has become part of everyday life. With a few clicks we can buy almost anything, and the goods often arrive the next day. The convenience is obvious, especially for people who live far from city centres. However, this habit also brings problems. Advertisements are designed to make us buy things we do not need, and low prices sometimes hide poor quality. I have learned to compare several shops before paying and to read comments carefully. Shopping online is neither good nor bad in itself; it depends on whether we stay sensible and control our desires.

essays.title: Food Waste on Campus
essays.text: In our canteen, large amounts of food are thrown away every day. Some students order more than they can eat simply because the dishes look attractive. This waste is difficult to accept when we remember that many people around the world still suffer from hunger. Our school has started a campaign to encourage reasonable portions. Students are asked to take only what they need and to finish everything on the plate. The change is small, but the message is important: respecting food means respecting the labour behind it. If we learn this lesson at school, we will carry it for the rest of our lives.

essays.title: A Low-carbon Lifestyle
essays.text: A low-carbon lifestyle does not require great sacrifice. It begins with ordinary decisions. I usually go to school by bike, which saves energy and keeps me fit. At home we use energy-saving lamps and turn off appliances that are not in use. We also try to repair things instead of replacing them immediately. Some people argue that individual actions are too small to affect the climate. I understand the doubt, but I believe that habits spread quickly. When your neighbours notice that your electricity bill is lower, they may copy you. A responsible society is built by individuals, not by slogans.

essays.title: The Music I Grew Up With
essays.text: Music has accompanied me since childhood. My mother used to play soft songs while cooking, and those melodies still make me feel safe. As a teenager I preferred loud bands, and my taste changed again when I discovered classical pieces. I do not think one kind of music is superior to another. What matters is the emotion it creates. When I feel stressed before an examination, a quiet piano piece can calm me down within minutes. Music also connects people: at a concert, thousands of strangers share the same feeling at the same moment. That experience is difficult to describe in words.

essays.title: Why I Play Basketball
essays.text: I have played basketball for four years, and it has taught me far more than how to shoot. On the court you must observe your teammates, make quick decisions and accept the result, whether it is victory or defeat. I remember a match in which we were behind by twelve points. Nobody believed we could win, but we kept passing and encouraging one another, and finally we succeeded. Sport is not only about physical strength. It develops cooperation, patience and courage. After an hour of exercise, my mind is clearer and my worries seem smaller. That is why I never regard it as a waste of study time.

essays.title: How I Learned English
essays.text: When I started learning English, I depended on translation and memorized long lists of words. I could pass tests but could not hold a conversation. Then my teacher advised me to read simple stories every day. At first it was slow and frustrating, because I looked up almost every word. After several months, however, I noticed that I could guess the meaning from the context. I also began to listen to short recordings while walking to school. Progress was invisible day by day but obvious year by year. The key is not talent; it is steady practice and a willingness to make mistakes.

essays.title: Traffic and Patience
essays.text: Rush hour in my city is a good test of character. Cars, bicycles and pedestrians compete for limited space, and tempers often become short. Some drivers ignore traffic lights and create dangerous situations. Others wait patiently and let pedestrians cross first. I once saw an old man fall from his bicycle at a busy crossing. Within seconds, several strangers stopped to help him and guided the traffic around. That moment impressed me more than any speech about civilization. Rules are necessary, but kindness is what makes a city truly livable.

essays.title: City Life and Country Life
essays.text: People often argue about whether it is better to live in a city or in the countryside. A city offers more opportunities: better schools, convenient transport and various entertainment. Yet it also brings noise, pollution and pressure. The countryside, by contrast, is quiet and close to nature, but medical services and job choices are limited. In my opinion, there is no perfect answer. The decision depends on a person's stage of life. A young graduate may need the energy of a city, while an elderly couple may prefer a peaceful village. What we should do is improve both, rather than look down on either.

essays.title: The Lesson of Manual Work
essays.text: Last month our school arranged a week of labour practice. We cleaned classrooms, planted vegetables and repaired broken chairs. Some students complained that such work had nothing to do with examinations. I disagreed. While sweeping the floor, I realized how much effort is hidden behind an ordinary clean room. When I tried to repair a chair, I discovered that patience and accuracy matter as much as knowledge. Manual work teaches respect for others' labour. It also reminds us that a society cannot run on ideas alone; somebody must do the practical work, and that work deserves dignity.

essays.title: Honesty Is a Choice
essays.text: Honesty is easy to praise and difficult to practise. Last term I found a wallet in the corridor. Nobody was watching, and I hesitated for a moment. Finally I handed it to the teacher, and the owner, a nervous freshman, thanked me repeatedly. The experience made me think about how often we face similar choices. Copying homework, hiding a mistake or exaggerating an achievement may bring temporary advantage, but they damage trust. Trust is difficult to build and easy to destroy. Being honest does not guarantee success, but it allows you to look at yourself without shame.

essays.title: The Value of Curiosity
essays.text: Children ask questions constantly, but as they grow older many of them stop. They become afraid of looking foolish or of wasting time. I think this change is a loss. Curiosity is the beginning of all learning. When I was preparing a report about the moon, I began to wonder how tides are formed. One question led to another, and I ended up reading far more than my teacher required. The information I gathered was not in any examination, yet it changed the way I see the world. We should protect curiosity instead of treating it as a distraction.

essays.title: The Importance of Sleep
essays.text: Many students treat sleep as something that can be reduced when work piles up. They stay up late, drink coffee and believe they are being productive. In fact, the opposite is often true. Without enough sleep, memory weakens, attention drops and moods become unstable. I once studied until two in the morning before an examination and performed worse than usual. Now I set a fixed bedtime and keep my phone outside the bedroom. My grades have improved and I feel more energetic. Rest is not a reward for finishing work; it is a condition for doing work well.

essays.title: Handling Pressure
essays.text: Pressure is a normal part of student life. Deadlines, competitions and expectations from parents can make us feel that we are never good enough. I used to hide my anxiety, believing that admitting it would make me weak. Later I learned that sharing a problem often reduces it. Talking with a friend, taking a walk or writing down my worries helps me see the situation more clearly. We cannot remove pressure entirely, but we can change how we respond to it. A calm mind is not a luxury; it is a basic tool for learning.

essays.title: Treating Others with Respect
essays.text: Respect is shown in small details. It means listening when someone is speaking, thanking the person who serves your meal, and not laughing at a classmate's accent. I once witnessed a new student being teased because of his clothes. He said nothing, but his face turned red. Later I sat beside him and we became friends. He told me that the teasing made him afraid to speak in class. Words that seem funny to one person can wound another deeply. Before making a joke, we should ask ourselves how we would feel in that position.

essays.title: Protecting Wild Animals
essays.text: Wild animals are disappearing at an alarming rate. Forests are cut down, rivers are polluted and natural habitats shrink year by year. Some species may vanish before scientists have a chance to study them. This is not only a problem for animals; it is a problem for human beings, because every species plays a role in the balance of nature. Individuals can help by refusing products made from endangered animals and by supporting organizations that protect them. Governments must also enforce laws strictly. The earth is not ours alone, and we have no right to destroy it for short-term profit.

essays.title: Exploring Space
essays.text: Space exploration once seemed like a competition between superpowers. Today it involves many countries and even private companies. Supporters argue that research in space produces useful technology, from satellite navigation to medical devices. Critics say the money should be spent on problems on earth, such as poverty and disease. Both views have some truth. In my opinion, exploration is part of human nature; we have always looked at the sky and wondered what lies beyond. The wise approach is to keep curiosity alive while making sure that the benefits are shared fairly.

essays.title: Chinese Food and Its Stories
essays.text: Chinese food is far more than a way to fill the stomach. Every dish carries a story. Dumplings, for example, are shaped like ancient money and symbolize good fortune. During festivals, families gather to prepare food together, and the process matters as much as the taste. Regional differences are striking: northern dishes tend to be salty, while southern cooking often uses sweetness. When foreigners taste our food, they are also tasting our history. That is why protecting traditional recipes is important. If a dish disappears, a piece of cultural memory disappears with it.

essays.title: The Subject I Enjoy Most
essays.text: Among all the subjects, literature is the one that attracts me most. Some classmates assume it is useless, yet I find it powerful. When we read a novel, we do not simply follow a plot; we enter another person's life and observe the world from a different angle. Our teacher often asks us to focus on how an author describes a scene rather than on what happens. This technique helps me understand why a character behaves in a particular way. I have learned to express my own feelings with greater accuracy. Literature may not earn me immediate marks, but it gives me a lifelong ability to understand people.

essays.title: Learning from Experts
essays.text: Young people often believe that they know better than adults. I used to hold this belief until I met my grandfather's colleague, an engineer with forty years of experience. He explained that a bridge is not designed by inspiration alone; every decision depends on evidence, careful analysis and repeated testing. His attitude impressed me. Experts are not always right, and we should not accept every opinion without question. However, ignoring experience simply because it is old is equally foolish. The wise approach is to listen, ask specific questions, and then form our own judgement based on facts rather than pride.

essays.title: The Rise of Short Videos
essays.text: Short videos have taken over our free time. A single clip lasts less than a minute, yet many students spend hours scrolling without noticing. Supporters argue that these videos spread knowledge quickly and give ordinary people a chance to be seen. Critics point out that constant switching weakens our ability to concentrate on anything longer than a minute. I belong to neither extreme. The technology itself is neutral; the problem lies in how we use it. If we set a clear time limit and choose content with real value, short videos can be a useful tool rather than a trap.

essays.title: Protection Starts with Awareness
essays.text: Many people claim to care about the environment, but their daily behaviour tells a different story. They buy unnecessary products, waste water and throw away food without a second thought. The gap between belief and action is the real problem. Environmental protection does not demand heroic sacrifice. It demands awareness: noticing how much you consume, where your rubbish goes and whether a product will last. Schools can help by organising visits to recycling centres, where students see the consequences with their own eyes. Once people understand the connection between their choices and the result, behaviour begins to change naturally.

essays.title: A Challenge I Faced
essays.text: Two years ago I was asked to give a speech in front of the whole school. I had never spoken to an audience of more than thirty people, and I was terrified. For a week I could hardly sleep. Instead of avoiding the challenge, I decided to prepare carefully: I wrote the draft, recorded myself, and asked a friend to listen and point out my weaknesses. On the day, my voice shook at first, but I finished. I did not win any prize, yet I gained something more valuable — the knowledge that fear can be managed through preparation.

essays.title: The Generation Gap
essays.text: The conflict between generations is as old as human society. Parents worry that their children are addicted to screens, while teenagers complain that adults do not understand their world. In my family, we once argued about whether I should attend an extra class during the holiday. Neither side was completely wrong. My parents focused on my future, and I focused on my need for rest. What helped was an honest conversation in which both of us explained our reasons. The gap does not disappear, but it becomes manageable when each side is willing to listen instead of simply insisting.

essays.title: Museums in a Digital Age
essays.text: Some people predict that museums will disappear because everything can be seen online. I doubt this. A photograph can show you the shape of an ancient pot, but it cannot show you its weight, its texture or the silence of the hall around it. Museums offer an experience that a screen cannot replace. At the same time, digital tools are valuable. Virtual tours allow students in remote areas to visit exhibitions they could never reach. The wise approach is cooperation: technology extends access, while the physical collection preserves the original object and its history.

essays.title: Food and Mood
essays.text: What we eat affects not only our body but also our mind. Research indicates that a diet rich in vegetables and fish helps people maintain a stable mood, while too much sugar may increase anxiety. I noticed this in my own life. During exam weeks I used to survive on instant noodles and coffee, and I felt tired and irritable. After I began to eat proper meals with fruit and vegetables, my energy improved and I could focus for longer periods. Healthy eating is not about strict rules; it is about giving your brain the fuel it needs to function.

essays.title: Volunteering in the Community
essays.text: Last winter I joined a programme that delivered meals to elderly residents in my neighbourhood. Many of them live alone, and for some, our visit was the only conversation of the day. At first I thought I was offering help. Gradually I realized that I was also receiving something. They told stories about the city before it changed, and their patience taught me to slow down. Volunteering is often described as a duty, but it can also be a form of education. It connects generations and reminds young people that a community is built through small, regular acts of care.

essays.title: Are We Losing Our Attention?
essays.text: Many teachers complain that students can no longer read a long article without losing focus. The average attention span seems to shrink every decade. Smartphones are usually blamed, and there is some truth in this. Every notification competes for our attention, and the brain gradually adapts to constant stimulation. However, blaming technology alone is too simple. We also need to examine our habits. Reading a book for thirty minutes a day is a form of training. Like any muscle, attention improves with practice and weakens without it.

essays.title: The Meaning of Success
essays.text: Success is usually measured by income, title or reputation. These standards are easy to count, which is why society relies on them. Yet they tell us little about a person's real life. I know a teacher who earns a modest salary but has influenced hundreds of students. I also know people with impressive positions who feel empty. In my opinion, success should be defined by whether your work has meaning for others and whether you can look at yourself honestly. This definition is harder to measure, but it is far more likely to lead to a satisfying life.

essays.title: Making Friends in a New School
essays.text: When I moved to a new school, I assumed that friendships would form automatically. They did not. For the first month I sat alone during lunch, convinced that everyone else already had their groups. Then a classmate asked me to join a study session, and everything changed. I learned that friendship rarely happens by chance; it requires a small act of courage from someone. Being the one who speaks first is uncomfortable, but it is often appreciated more than we imagine. Looking back, the hardest part was not the new environment but my own assumption that I did not belong.
